label: Shofetim (Judges) — Part 2 — Chapters 8–14
summary_plain: After Gid'on's victory, the people ask him to rule over them — he refuses: YHWH will rule over you. But Gid'on makes a golden ephod that becomes a snare. His son Avimelekh murders seventy brothers and makes himself king at Shekhem — the first Israelite to claim kingship by force. Yotam speaks the parable of the trees. YHWH raises Yiftach as judge — he makes a rash vow. Shimshon is born — a Nazirite from the womb, whose strength comes from YHWH.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from 4QJudg-a, 4QJudg-b and the Orit Ge'ez. Gid'on's refusal of kingship (8:23) is the clearest statement of theocratic principle in the pre-monarchic period. Avimelekh's self-made kingship at Shekhem (ch 9) is the anti-model — human power seized without YHWH's appointment. Shimshon's Nazirite dedication (ch 13) connects to the Bamidbar 6 Nazirite laws.

key_terms.definition: The son of Gid'on and a Shekhem concubine who murders 70 of his brothers on one stone to seize rule over Shekhem. His name means 'my father is king' — the irony being that Gid'on refused the kingship but his son takes it by force. Avimelekh rules three years and dies when a woman drops a millstone on his head from a tower wall.

In Shofetim 9, the one surviving brother (Yotam) stands on Mount Gerizim and tells a parable: the trees seek a king; the olive tree, fig tree, and vine all refuse (they have better things to do); only the bramble agrees — and the bramble threatens to burn down the cedars of Levanon. The parable exposes the worthlessness of Avimelekh's rule and the people's foolishness in choosing him.

The son of Gilead and a prostitute, driven away by his legitimate brothers. When Ammon threatens, the elders of Gilead bring him back and commission him as leader. He negotiates with Ammon diplomatically before fighting, makes a rash vow before the battle, and defeats Ammon. His vow then destroys his only child.

Before the battle against Ammon, Yiftah vows to YHWH: 'Whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace... I will offer it up as a burnt offering.' His daughter — his only child — comes out first with tambourines. The text presents his grief and her acceptance without condemning him or resolving the theological tension.

Unnamed in the text, she receives the vow without protest, asks only for two months to mourn her virginity in the hills with her companions, then returns. The daughters of Yisra'el afterward go four days a year to mourn her — an annual lament preserved in Yisra'el's covenant memory. She is the innocent victim of her father's rash oath.

The last judge named before Shmu'el — a Nazirite from birth (his mother given the vow before he was born), who delivers Yisra'el from the Philistines through personal feats of strength. His power is tied to his Nazirite status (the uncut hair), and his fatal flaw is his attraction to Philistine women, which repeatedly compromises him.

At his wedding feast to a Philistine woman, Shimshon poses a riddle about honey found in a lion's carcass: 'Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet.' The Philistine guests coerce his wife into extracting the answer. When they give it, Shimshon knows they cheated, and he pays the wager by killing 30 Philistines and taking their garments.

A vow consecrating a person to YHWH (Bamidbar 6): no cutting of hair, no grape products, no contact with corpses. For Shimshon, the vow was set before his birth by YHWH's messenger. His uncut hair is the visible sign of his consecration and the source of his supernatural strength — not magic but covenant sign. When the hair is cut, the sign is broken and YHWH's presence departs.

The word used in Shofetim 12 to identify Efrayimites fleeing after Yiftah's battle with them. The Gileadites at the Jordan crossing asked each man to say 'shibboleth' (a grain stalk). Efrayim's dialect could not produce the 'sh' sound, so they said 'sibboleth.' 42,000 Efrayimites were killed by this linguistic test.

Avimelekh's death in Shofetim 9: he attacks the tower at Tevetz and approaches the door to set it on fire. A woman drops an upper millstone on his head, fatally wounding him. Aware he is dying, he commands his armor-bearer to run him through with a sword 'lest they say a woman killed him.' Yotam's curse ('may YHWH judge between Avimelekh and the men of Shekhem') is fulfilled. YHWH repaid his evil.

faq.question: What does Yotam's parable say about the nature of power?
faq.answer: Yotam's parable is the Tanakh's most direct political critique. The worthy trees — olive, fig, vine — all refuse to be king because they have genuine purpose: oil, sweetness, wine 'that cheers' the Creator and human beings. Only the bramble, which produces nothing of value, agrees to be king, and immediately threatens destruction. The parable's argument: those who seek power are precisely those who should not have it; those who should lead have better things to do. Avimelekh is the bramble — useless, dangerous, capable only of burning down what others built. The parable is preserved as covenant wisdom about leadership selection.

faq.question: Is Yiftah's vow a tragedy or a covenant violation?
faq.answer: The text presents it as both without resolving the tension. Yiftah clearly did not intend to vow his daughter — he vowed 'whatever comes out of my house,' likely expecting an animal. He tore his clothes and said 'you have brought me very low.' But the vow was made in YHWH's name, and the daughter affirms it must be kept: 'Do to me what you have vowed — YHWH has given you victory.' The annual lament of the daughters of Yisra'el treats her death as a genuine tragedy worth communal mourning. The Torah's provision against rash vows (Bamidbar 30) exists precisely because vows spoken in YHWH's name carry binding weight regardless of consequences. The text holds the tension: vows are serious; this one was rash; both things are true.

faq.question: What does Shimshon's story say about the Nazirite consecration?
faq.answer: Shimshon was consecrated before birth — his mother received the commission from YHWH's messenger before he was conceived. This makes his case different from voluntary Nazirite vows: Shimshon did not choose consecration, he was born into it. His strength is explicitly tied to the Nazirite sign: when his hair is cut, the text says 'YHWH had left him.' The hair is not magical — it is a covenant sign. When the sign is broken (through his own disclosure to Delilah), the covenant presence that enabled his strength withdraws. Shimshon's story is a sustained illustration of what happens when covenant consecration is treated casually.

faq.question: Why is the Shibboleth story significant beyond its immediate use?
faq.answer: The Shibboleth episode (the Efrayim-Gilead conflict in Shofetim 12) is the first documented instance in human record of a linguistic test used for lethal identification. 42,000 people died because of a sound they could not produce. The episode also reveals intra-Israelite violence: this is not Yisra'el against Ammon but tribe against tribe. After Yiftah's victory over Ammon, Efrayim came to claim credit and threatened Yiftah. The civil war that followed and the Jordan crossing test demonstrate how the judges period's covenant breakdown was not only about foreign oppression but about Yisra'el tearing itself apart.

faq.question: What does the annual lament for Yiftah's daughter mean?
faq.answer: The daughters of Yisra'el went four days each year to lament. This is a formal covenant memory practice — a recognized communal ritual preserving the memory of an injustice that could not be undone. It is striking that she is never named in the text; she is remembered only through the practice of remembrance itself. The annual lament is Yisra'el's honest accounting of what rash vows cost. Covenant memory is not selective — it includes failures and innocent victims alongside victories. The daughters preserving this memory may be one of the most remarkable acts of corporate covenant honesty in Shofetim.

faq.question: How does Avimelekh's death fulfill Yotam's curse?
faq.answer: When Yotam delivered his parable from Mount Gerizim, he ended with a formal curse: 'If you have acted in bad faith... let fire come out from Avimelekh and devour the men of Shekhem, and let fire come out from the men of Shekhem and devour Avimelekh.' The book records exactly that: Shekhem rebelled against Avimelekh, he burned the tower of Shekhem killing a thousand people, then he was killed by a millstone at the tower of Tevetz. The text explicitly notes: 'Thus YHWH repaid the evil of Avimelekh... and also all the evil of the men of Shekhem YHWH returned on their heads.' Covenant curses spoken in YHWH's name are fulfilled.

faq.question: Who was Jephthah before he became a judge?
faq.answer: Yiftah was the illegitimate son of Gilead and a prostitute. His legitimate brothers drove him away: 'You shall not inherit in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman.' He fled to the land of Tov and gathered a band of worthless men around him. When Ammon threatened, the elders of Gilead came to him — the same community that had expelled him. Yiftah negotiated his terms: 'If you bring me home to fight Ammon and YHWH gives them to me, I will be your head.' The pattern is consistent with Shofetim: YHWH chooses the rejected, the outcast, the last in line. Yiftah's social marginalization is the qualification, not an obstacle.

faq.question: What does Shimshon's engagement with Philistine women mean for his story?
faq.answer: Shimshon is called by YHWH to 'begin to save Yisra'el from the hand of the Philistines,' but he pursues Philistine women three times. His father objects to his first marriage: 'Is there not a woman among all our people, that you go to get a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?' The text notes YHWH was behind it: 'his father and mother did not know it was from YHWH.' This introduces a troubling element: YHWH uses Shimshon's personal weakness as an instrument for confronting the Philistines. The theology is not clean. Shimshon is a covenant instrument whose fatal flaw is simultaneously his means of engagement with the enemy. His story resists tidy moral categories.

faq.question: What is the significance of Avimelekh dying at a woman's hand?
faq.answer: The death by millstone is covenant irony piled on covenant irony. Gid'on refused the kingship Yisra'el offered. His son Avimelekh seized it by killing 70 brothers on one stone. He dies with his skull crushed by a woman throwing an upper millstone. He commands his armor-bearer to finish him 'lest they say a woman killed me' — but the text records exactly that: the woman killed him. His final act was trying to suppress the truth of his end. YHWH repaid his evil through the instrument Avimelekh most feared and least respected. The military glory Avimelekh sought ended at a woman's hand, with his own sword completing what she started.

faq.question: How does the Jephthah episode advance the theme of words and covenant?
faq.answer: Covenant speech in Shofetim carries fatal weight. Yotam speaks a curse from Mount Gerizim and it is fulfilled. Yiftah speaks a vow and his daughter dies from it. The book is tracking what happens when covenant language is handled carelessly. YHWH's covenant is verbal — it was established through his words to Avraham, Yitzhak, Ya'akov, Mosheh. Human speech that invokes YHWH's name participates in that covenant reality. Yiftah's vow was not theologically defective — the problem was speaking without thinking. The annual lament is Yisra'el's liturgical acknowledgment that they know what unthinking covenant speech costs.
